extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, state regulators, electric utilities (especially distribution cooperatives), and stakeholders preparing comments on Section 111(d) GHG rule
extracted.subtask_description: Drafting or evaluating comments and guidance on EPA’s proposed use of end-use energy efficiency (EE) as part of Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) under Clean Air Act Section 111(d), with emphasis on state flexibility, costs, EM&V, and impacts on distribution cooperatives and rural customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State authority and unit-specific analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: States, not EPA, should determine whether and how to implement EE programs and set standards of performance for each existing source within their borders; EPA must allow States to conduct the unit-specific analysis the statute contemplates rather than imposing uniform assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States need flexibility to set goals based on unique circumstances and state-specific data; EPA should not arbitrarily assume all regulated sources can achieve uniform limits or require some sources to overachieve to offset others. (See: “States and not the EPA should determine whether and, if so, how to implement EE programs… EPA does not allow a State to conduct the unit-specific analysis…”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uniform statewide EE targets that ignore utility heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s uniform 1.5% annual EE savings target fails to account for broad differences across and within States (e.g., investor-owned utilities vs. distribution cooperatives) that determine what is cost-effective, achievable, and sustainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target-setting should reflect variation among utilities; examples: Arizona discounted standards for distribution cooperatives and Arizona waivers when utilities could not meet standards. NRECA-commissioned analysis found many individual utilities cannot meet a 1.5% goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic target setting based on historical achievement and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: EE goals must be realistic relative to how long leading States took to achieve particular annual savings levels; EPA’s proposed deadlines are often much shorter than historical experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s proposal compressed timelines (e.g., less than half the time it took leading States to achieve 1.5%); only one State has achieved over 2% — so higher nationwide goals (e.g., 2.0%) are unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for significant upfront and ongoing costs to States, utilities, and consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s analysis must account for the substantial upfront costs to States and program administrators, and the direct and indirect costs borne by consumers — particularly in rural and low-income areas served by cooperatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperatives often have limited resources, low customer density, higher per-customer program costs, and serve high-poverty areas and mobile homes; costs borne by consumers (via higher bills) should be explicitly modeled rather than assumed negligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use realistic Levelized Cost of Saved Energy (LCSE) estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s LCSE estimates are understated; the economics literature and program experience indicate higher LCSEs and escalation over time as programs scale up and low-cost opportunities are exhausted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s high-end 2017 estimate of ~9.9 ¢/kWh (3%/7% discount assumptions) understates national and administrator medians (e.g., LBNL median residential costs are much higher); EPA should consider higher LCSEs and rising marginal costs over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize cost-sharing and cooperatives’ business model implications
rubrics_metrics.description: EE program design must explicitly recognize that program costs are typically split between administrators and consumers, and that co-ops’ nonprofit/member-owned model means costs translate directly to member-consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because cooperatives cannot easily shift costs, higher administrative costs translate to higher bills for member-owners; EPA should reflect who ultimately bears costs when assessing benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for consumer behavior and higher private discount rates
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must account for behavioral barriers and much higher 'private' discount rates among residential (and low-income) consumers that reduce adoption of EE measures absent substantially higher incentives and outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While administrators might use 3–7% discount rates, consumers may face private discount rates ~15–25% (e.g., credit card financing at ~20%); blended rates raise LCSE. EPA should model adoption frictions, need for education/incentives, and higher admin spending required to increase uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use realistic measure-life assumptions for EE measures
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s assumption of a 20-year measure life for efficiency improvements is often optimistic; many lighting and HVAC measures have shorter effective lives due to failure or early retirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter measure lives increase LCSE and reduce lifetime savings; EPA should review measure-life studies (e.g., GDS Associates/DEER) and apply measure-life ranges appropriate to measure types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume automatic consumer adoption ('if States build it, they will adopt')
rubrics_metrics.description: EE programs have historically been voluntary and incentive-driven; many consumers and businesses will not adopt measures even when offered, especially during economic downturns or when out-of-pocket costs are high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should model adoption rates that reflect voluntary program realities, economic cycles, and evidence that observed EE gains may be driven by reduced demand rather than program participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit early actions and existing state EE programs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s baseline and target-setting must credit reductions that States and utilities have already achieved through prior EE investments; failing to credit early action penalizes states that invested earlier and discourages voluntary programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Colorado’s Energy Performance Contracting invested $447.4M yet EPA’s data showed only 0.84% annual savings; EPA should allow states to adjust goals to reflect prior investments and low-cost measures already implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating kWh reductions directly to CO2 reductions without accounting for generation mix
rubrics_metrics.description: End-use electricity savings do not necessarily yield the assumed greenhouse gas reductions because displaced generation may be zero- or low-carbon, or avoided kWh may not reduce generation in the expected location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must analyze the generation mix and marginal dispatch effects (e.g., displacement of nuclear, wind, hydro, or gas) rather than assume a direct kWh-to-CO2 mapping; otherwise state emission goals are arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly evaluate and account for the rebound effect
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should properly assess direct and indirect rebound effects wherein efficiency gains lower effective energy costs and may increase energy consumption (e.g., increased use for comfort) or increase energy use elsewhere in the economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s dismissal of rebound as 'relatively modest' is insufficient; rebound could materially affect emissions outcomes and must be incorporated into target-setting and benefit estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address geographic mismatch: EE adoption in one State with affected generation in another
rubrics_metrics.description: EE measures implemented in one State may result in reduced generation (and emissions) in another State; EPA cannot assume in-state emissions reductions without accounting for cross-border impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target-setting and crediting approaches must handle interstate flows and location of marginal generation, or risk attributing nonexistent in-state emission reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hold utilities accountable for reductions they cannot control
rubrics_metrics.description: If utilities (especially distribution cooperatives) have no role in developing or implementing EE programs, it is unreasonable and unfair to tie compliance obligations to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement and compliance responsibilities should be aligned with entities that implement the programs; States should avoid requiring utilities to meet reductions they do not control or influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave EM&V protocol design to States and allow unit-by-unit flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Protocols for evaluation, measurement, and verification (EM&V) of end-use EE should be state-determined and tailored to utility size, resources, and customer base rather than federally mandated one-size-fits-all protocols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should not presume existing state EM&V protocols are preferred for other states; permit unit-by-unit flexibility and simpler methodologies where appropriate. A 'small utilities protocol' approach is an example of tailoring to smaller utilities' needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow simpler, cost-effective EM&V methods (avoid IOU-centric paradigms)
rubrics_metrics.description: EM&V designed for large IOUs (large sample sizes, rigorous statistical analysis, in-home visits) can be overly costly and unnecessary for many programs; states should be able to use upstream or higher-level monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologies should strike a balance between cost and benefit; where available, use technical reference manuals, deemed savings, program impact evaluations, and other existing sources to reduce EM&V costs and realize economies of scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require mandatory third-party verification/certification for EE programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandatory third-party verification/certification of EE programs would significantly increase program costs and build-out time without commensurate benefits, particularly for smaller utilities and cooperatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing compliance requirements and state oversight can ensure adequate evaluation and verification; third-party mandates should be avoided to prevent prohibitive costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for erosion/non-persistence of EE savings over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy savings from EE measures may not persist due to remodeling, equipment replacement, changes in occupancy, weather-driven changes in usage, or poor maintenance; persistence risk must be accounted for in analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should incorporate persistence/lifetime risk into savings estimates (not assume permanent savings) and recognize that such non-persistence reduces the reliability of EE as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize increasing marginal costs after early action (low-hanging fruit exhausted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial EE gains capture low-cost measures; as programs mature, remaining potential is costlier per unit saved and percent savings tend to decline year-on-year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should model declining year-on-year savings and increasing marginal costs; historical trends (e.g., decreasing percent EE savings for cooperatives after initial years) demonstrate this effect and should inform target trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include waiver mechanisms or discounted standards where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where original standards exceed what individual utilities can reasonably attain, State-level waiver processes or discounted standards (as Arizona EERS did for distribution cooperatives) are appropriate and necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule design should allow states to implement waiver procedures and discounted targets to reflect realistic attainability and prevent overburdening smaller or resource-constrained utilities.
